paragraphs.title: Fear of the Amorite and Canaanite kings

easy.question: Who heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the Israelites?
answers: The kings of the Amorites and the kings of the Canaanites
The kings of Egypt
The prophets of Israel
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly says 'all the kings of the Amorites... and all the kings of the Canaanites' heard of the act.

easy.question: What did the LORD do to the waters of the Jordan according to the verse?
answers: He moved them to another sea
He dried them up
He turned them into a sea of blood
easy.explanation: The verse says 'that the LORD had dried up the waters of Jordan' — the waters were dried up.

easy.question: What happened to the hearts of the kings when they heard this?
answers: They were filled with joy
They traveled to make a treaty
Their hearts melted and they were afraid
easy.explanation: The phrase 'their heart melted' expresses fear and loss of courage.

medium.question: Why did the kings' hearts melt according to the verse?
answers: Because the LORD dried up the Jordan and the Israelites crossed
Because they heard their kingdom was dissolving
Because the Jordan was flooded with harmful waters
medium.explanation: The verse links the drying of the Jordan and Israel's crossing with the kings' loss of courage.

medium.question: What is reported immediately after the drying of the waters?
answers: That the kings sent envoys to request peace
That their hearts melted and they lost courage because of the Israelites
That surrounding nations made a covenant with Israel
medium.explanation: The verse continues to describe the kings' reaction: their hearts melted and there was no more spirit in them because of Israel.

medium.question: What does 'their heart melted' mean in this context?
answers: Their hearts hardened and strengthened
They began to dance with joy
Their courage failed and they were afraid
medium.explanation: Here 'melted' signifies a weakening of heart — the verse adds 'neither was there spirit in them any more,' showing fear and loss of courage.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'which were on the side of Jordan westward' indicate about the location of those kings?
answers: On the other side of the Jordan toward the sea — i.e., west of the Jordan
East of the Jordan
North of the Jordan
challenge.explanation: The phrase describes the region toward the sea, i.e., across the Jordan in the direction of the sea (west).

challenge.question: When it says 'neither was there spirit in them any more', what does the verse most likely mean?
answers: That they actually died
That they lost courage and will to resist
That they made a peace treaty
challenge.explanation: This expression typically indicates loss of courage or will to fight — i.e., fear and demoralization.

challenge.question: According to the verse, who caused the drying up of the waters of Jordan?
answers: Heavy natural rain
Joshua and the people of Israel
The LORD
challenge.explanation: The verse attributes the act to the LORD: 'that the LORD had dried up the waters'.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'which were on the side of Jordan westward' indicate about the location of those kings?
answers: On the other side of the Jordan toward the sea — i.e., west of the Jordan
East of the Jordan
North of the Jordan
questions.explanation: The phrase describes the region toward the sea, i.e., across the Jordan in the direction of the sea (west).

questions.question: When it says 'neither was there spirit in them any more', what does the verse most likely mean?
answers: That they actually died
That they lost courage and will to resist
That they made a peace treaty
questions.explanation: This expression typically indicates loss of courage or will to fight — i.e., fear and demoralization.

answers: Heavy natural rain
Joshua and the people of Israel
The LORD
questions.explanation: The verse attributes the act to the LORD: 'that the LORD had dried up the waters'.

easy.question: Who spoke to Joshua in verse 2?
answers: The LORD
Moses
The people
easy.explanation: The verse opens 'At that time the LORD said unto Joshua' — it is the LORD speaking.

easy.question: What did the LORD command Joshua to make?
answers: To build an altar
Make thee sharp knives
Send a delegation
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly says 'Make thee sharp knives' — the command is to prepare sharp knives.

easy.question: What was done to the Israelites in verse 3?
answers: They were sent to build
They were killed
They were circumcised
easy.explanation: Verse 3 states 'And Joshua circumcised the children of Israel' — they were circumcised.

medium.question: Why were the sharp knives made according to the text?
answers: To fight enemies
To perform a sacrifice
To circumcise the Israelites
medium.explanation: The making of the knives is mentioned together with the circumcision — they were tools for the procedure.

medium.question: What does the verb 'circumcised' mean in the context 'And he circumcised the children of Israel'?
answers: Performed the covenant of circumcision (removed foreskins)
To count the Israelites
To send messengers
medium.explanation: 'Circumcise' here refers to the covenantal act of removing the foreskin (the rite of circumcision).

medium.question: Who carried out the acts (making the knives and circumcising the people) according to the verse?
answers: The people themselves
Joshua
The priests
medium.explanation: The verse says 'And Joshua made... and circumcised the children of Israel' — Joshua performed the actions.

challenge.question: What can we infer about the Israelites' condition before the circumcision episodes?
answers: They were already under the covenant of circumcision
They were uncircumcised
They had lived in the land for many generations
challenge.explanation: The account at 'the hill of the foreskins' implies many were uncircumcised until that event.

challenge.question: In the phrase 'Make thee sharp knives', what kind of cutting tools does the verse most likely refer to in the ancient context?
answers: Knives made of copper
Advanced metal swords
Cutting tools made of flint/stone
challenge.explanation: The term 'sharp knives' in the ancient context likely denotes cutting tools made from flint or stone rather than advanced metal swords.

challenge.question: What does the name 'the hill of the foreskins' indicate about the place?
answers: A specific site where the uncircumcised were gathered to be circumcised
Name of a large capital city
A river that crossed the camp
challenge.explanation: The name marks the specific location where the uncircumcised were brought to be circumcised — hence the name.

questions.question: What can we infer about the Israelites' condition before the circumcision episodes?
answers: They were already under the covenant of circumcision
They were uncircumcised
They had lived in the land for many generations
questions.explanation: The account at 'the hill of the foreskins' implies many were uncircumcised until that event.

answers: Knives made of copper
Advanced metal swords
Cutting tools made of flint/stone
questions.explanation: The term 'sharp knives' in the ancient context likely denotes cutting tools made from flint or stone rather than advanced metal swords.

answers: A specific site where the uncircumcised were gathered to be circumcised

questions.explanation: The name marks the specific location where the uncircumcised were brought to be circumcised — hence the name.

paragraphs.title: The generation that did not circumcise and the act of circumcision

easy.question: What happened to all the fighting men who came out of Egypt?
answers: They stayed in Egypt
They died in the wilderness
They entered the land immediately
easy.explanation: Verse 4 states that all the men of war who came out of Egypt died in the wilderness on the way.

easy.question: Who had not been circumcised on the way when they came out of Egypt?
answers: All who came out of Egypt
The entire nation
Those born in the wilderness on the journey
easy.explanation: Verse 5 notes that those born in the wilderness as they went forth out of Egypt had not been circumcised.

easy.question: How many years did the Israelites travel in the wilderness?
answers: Forty years
Seven years
Twenty years
easy.explanation: Verse 6 explicitly says they walked forty years in the wilderness.

medium.question: What reason is given why the generation of fighting men did not see the land?
answers: Because they disobeyed the LORD and He swore they would not enter
Because lions in the wilderness killed them
Because of famine forcing them back to Egypt
medium.explanation: Verse 6 explains they 'obeyed not the voice of the LORD' and therefore the LORD swore they would not see the promised land.

medium.question: What does 'uncircumcised' mean in this context?
answers: Foreign people not Israelites
Ritually impure for other reasons
Those who had not been circumcised (not under the covenant)
medium.explanation: 'Uncircumcised' refers to males who had not undergone the covenantal rite of circumcision.

medium.question: Who performed the circumcision for the children born in the wilderness?
answers: Moses
Joshua
The elders
medium.explanation: Verse 7 states that Joshua circumcised them — Joshua performed the act.

challenge.question: What can we infer from the statement that they walked forty years in the wilderness until all the fighting men were consumed?
answers: There were no losses in battle for forty years
The generation that came out of Egypt died and was replaced by a new generation born in the wilderness
All the people entered the land unchanged after forty years
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates the older generation died over the forty years and the next generation remained to enter the land.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'a land that floweth with milk and honey' mean?
answers: A description of a fertile and prosperous land
A dry and desert land
The name of a specific city
challenge.explanation: The expression is a metaphor for a fertile, prosperous land — abundance and richness.

challenge.question: Why did they remain in the camp until they were healed after circumcision?
answers: To prepare weapons and perform more rituals
To arrange meetings with neighboring tribes
To recover from the wounds caused by the circumcision
challenge.explanation: The verse says they abode in their places in the camp until they were whole — i.e., until they healed from the circumcision.

questions.question: What can we infer from the statement that they walked forty years in the wilderness until all the fighting men were consumed?
answers: There were no losses in battle for forty years
The generation that came out of Egypt died and was replaced by a new generation born in the wilderness
All the people entered the land unchanged after forty years
questions.explanation: The phrase indicates the older generation died over the forty years and the next generation remained to enter the land.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'a land that floweth with milk and honey' mean?
answers: A description of a fertile and prosperous land
A dry and desert land
The name of a specific city
questions.explanation: The expression is a metaphor for a fertile, prosperous land — abundance and richness.

questions.question: Why did they remain in the camp until they were healed after circumcision?
answers: To prepare weapons and perform more rituals
To arrange meetings with neighboring tribes
To recover from the wounds caused by the circumcision
questions.explanation: The verse says they abode in their places in the camp until they were whole — i.e., until they healed from the circumcision.

paragraphs.title: Removing the reproach of Egypt and naming Gilgal

easy.question: Who spoke to Joshua in this verse?
answers: The LORD
Pharaoh
A neighboring king
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'And the LORD said unto Joshua' — it is God speaking to Joshua.

easy.question: What did the LORD say He had removed?
answers: The people's rest
The reproach of Egypt
The land's poverty
easy.explanation: The verse states 'This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you' — the 'reproach of Egypt' has been removed.

easy.question: What is the name given to that place?
answers: Jordan
Egypt
Gilgal
easy.explanation: The verse says the name of the place is called Gilgal.

medium.question: When does the LORD say He removed the reproach?
answers: The next day
At the time of the Exodus
This day
medium.explanation: The verse uses 'This day' — the LORD declares the reproach removed at that moment.

medium.question: What does the word 'reproach' mean in the phrase 'the reproach of Egypt'?
answers: Shame or dishonor
A gift or reward
The name of a place
medium.explanation: 'Reproach' here means shame or dishonor; the LORD says He removed the shame related to Egypt.

medium.question: Why was the place called Gilgal according to the verse?
answers: Because of a large wave of water there
Because the reproach of Egypt was removed and the name links to the idea of rolling away
Because an important figure was born there
medium.explanation: The verse connects the removal of the reproach with the naming: the name (Gilgal) is linked to the idea of rolling away.

challenge.question: What is the likely meaning of 'the reproach of Egypt' here?
answers: The wealth they stole from Egypt
The shame associated with Israel's time under Egypt
The land of Egypt itself
challenge.explanation: In biblical usage 'reproach' denotes shame or dishonor; the context refers to removing the shame tied to Egypt.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'and the name of that place was called Gilgal unto this day' imply?
answers: The place was destroyed soon after
The name was later forgotten
That the name 'Gilgal' was preserved and still called so in the narrator's time
challenge.explanation: 'Unto this day' in the Bible signals that the name continued to be used up to the narrator's time.

challenge.question: How does the verse link the action described to the place-name 'Gilgal'?
answers: It says the words are unrelated
It uses a verbal link between the act of 'rolling away' the reproach and the name 'Gilgal'
It calls Gilgal a person's name
challenge.explanation: The verse makes a linguistic/idea connection: the action of removing (rolling away) the reproach is tied to the place-name Gilgal.

questions.question: What is the likely meaning of 'the reproach of Egypt' here?
answers: The wealth they stole from Egypt
The shame associated with Israel's time under Egypt
The land of Egypt itself
questions.explanation: In biblical usage 'reproach' denotes shame or dishonor; the context refers to removing the shame tied to Egypt.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'and the name of that place was called Gilgal unto this day' imply?
answers: The place was destroyed soon after
The name was later forgotten
That the name 'Gilgal' was preserved and still called so in the narrator's time
questions.explanation: 'Unto this day' in the Bible signals that the name continued to be used up to the narrator's time.

questions.question: How does the verse link the action described to the place-name 'Gilgal'?
answers: It says the words are unrelated
It uses a verbal link between the act of 'rolling away' the reproach and the name 'Gilgal'
It calls Gilgal a person's name
questions.explanation: The verse makes a linguistic/idea connection: the action of removing (rolling away) the reproach is tied to the place-name Gilgal.

paragraphs.title: Passover at Jericho and eating of the produce

easy.question: Where did the Israelites camp according to verse 10?
answers: In Gilgal
In Jericho
At Beth El
easy.explanation: Verse 10 explicitly says 'the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal' — they camped at Gilgal.

easy.question: When did the Israelites keep the Passover?
answers: At evening on the fifteenth day
At evening on the fourteenth day
At dawn on the fourteenth day
easy.explanation: The verse says they kept the Passover 'on the fourteenth day of the month at even' — evening of the 14th.

easy.question: What did they eat the day after the Passover according to verse 11?
answers: Only the sacrificial meat
Only unleavened bread (matzot)
Unleavened bread and parched grain (old corn)
easy.explanation: Verse 11 reports they 'did eat unleavened cakes, and parched corn' — unleavened bread and parched grain.

medium.question: What does 'of the old corn of the land' mean in verse 11 in the context of the event?
answers: They began to eat the produce of the land instead of manna
Travelers passed through the land on the way
They only ate while traveling
medium.explanation: The phrase indicates they were eating the land's produce — not the manna — marking use of local crops.

medium.question: What does 'parched' mean in 'unleavened cakes, and parched corn'?
answers: Cooked in water
Roasted/parched grain (parched corn)
Leavened
medium.explanation: 'Parched' refers to grain roasted or dried — parched corn/grain, not leavened.

medium.question: What happened immediately after the Passover according to verses 10–11?
answers: They launched an immediate attack on Jericho
They returned to Sinai
The next day they ate unleavened bread and parched grain
medium.explanation: The verses describe that the day after the Passover they ate of the land — unleavened and parched grain.

challenge.question: What can be inferred from holding the Passover 'in the plains of Jericho'?
answers: That they were already inside Canaan and beginning to observe the laws there
That they planned a night surprise attack on Jericho
That they celebrated in a place unsuitable for Passover
challenge.explanation: Holding the Passover in the plains of Jericho shows they were in the territory of Canaan and began observing the festival there.

challenge.question: Geographically, how is Gilgal located relative to Jericho according to the phrase?
answers: On the Mediterranean coast
On a high mountain north of Jerusalem
In the plain near Jericho — 'the plains of Jericho'
challenge.explanation: The phrase 'in the plains of Jericho' describes a plain near Jericho; Gilgal is mentioned in that context.

challenge.question: What does the emphasis 'in the selfsame day' in verse 11 imply about their eating?
answers: They postponed eating to other days
They ate on that very day without delay
It indicates the food was only eaten at night
challenge.explanation: The phrase stresses that they ate on that very day — they did not delay eating the land's produce.

questions.question: What can be inferred from holding the Passover 'in the plains of Jericho'?
answers: That they were already inside Canaan and beginning to observe the laws there
That they planned a night surprise attack on Jericho
That they celebrated in a place unsuitable for Passover
questions.explanation: Holding the Passover in the plains of Jericho shows they were in the territory of Canaan and began observing the festival there.

questions.question: Geographically, how is Gilgal located relative to Jericho according to the phrase?
answers: On the Mediterranean coast
On a high mountain north of Jerusalem
In the plain near Jericho — 'the plains of Jericho'
questions.explanation: The phrase 'in the plains of Jericho' describes a plain near Jericho; Gilgal is mentioned in that context.

questions.question: What does the emphasis 'in the selfsame day' in verse 11 imply about their eating?
answers: They postponed eating to other days
They ate on that very day without delay
It indicates the food was only eaten at night
questions.explanation: The phrase stresses that they ate on that very day — they did not delay eating the land's produce.

paragraphs.title: The manna ceased and they ate the produce

easy.question: What ceased according to this verse?
answers: The manna
The produce of the land
The Israelites didn't eat
easy.explanation: The verse states 'And the manna ceased' — the manna stopped.

easy.question: When did the manna cease according to the verse?
answers: Before they ate of the land's produce
The next day after they had eaten
At the time of the Exodus
easy.explanation: The verse says 'and the manna ceased on the morrow after they had eaten of the old corn' — it ceased the next day.

easy.question: What did the Israelites eat instead of manna in that year?
answers: Meat from offerings
Food from heaven
The produce of the land of Canaan
easy.explanation: The verse says they 'did eat of the fruit of the land of Canaan' — they ate the land's produce.

medium.question: According to the verse, why did the manna stop?
answers: Because they ate the produce of the land
Because the LORD stopped sending tests
Because there were no people left to eat
medium.explanation: The verse links the cessation of manna to their eating of the land's produce: the manna ceased after they ate of the land.

medium.question: Which sequence of events is correct according to the verse?
answers: The manna stopped first, then they began to eat the land's produce
They ate from the land, and the next day the manna stopped
The manna and the land's produce appeared at the same time
medium.explanation: The verse indicates they ate of the land's produce and the next day the manna ceased — eating came first, then manna ended.

medium.question: What does the word 'produce' refer to in 'the produce of the land of Canaan'?
answers: A tax on agricultural produce
The yield of the land — its crops and fruits
An imported commodity
medium.explanation: 'Produce' here means the land's yield — crops and fruits from Canaan.

challenge.question: What does it mean for the Israelites that they ate of Canaan's produce that year?
answers: That they had already entered the land and it supplied their food
Their physical condition worsened and they stopped getting food
They returned to eating manna because there was no grain
challenge.explanation: Eating the land's produce indicates they were in Canaan and the land provided sufficient food so manna was no longer needed.

challenge.question: What does the use of 'no more' in 'there was no more manna' imply?
answers: That manna returned later for a short time
That from that moment on they would no longer use manna
That manna remained only partially
challenge.explanation: The phrase 'no more' signals that the manna ceased from that point onward — it was no longer given.

challenge.question: What characteristic of the land of Canaan is suggested by this verse?
answers: A desert land without grain
A fertile land whose produce could feed the people
An isolated region without agricultural economy
challenge.explanation: The verse portrays Canaan as fertile and productive — its produce could sustain the people.

questions.question: What does it mean for the Israelites that they ate of Canaan's produce that year?
answers: That they had already entered the land and it supplied their food
Their physical condition worsened and they stopped getting food
They returned to eating manna because there was no grain
questions.explanation: Eating the land's produce indicates they were in Canaan and the land provided sufficient food so manna was no longer needed.

answers: That manna returned later for a short time
That from that moment on they would no longer use manna
That manna remained only partially
questions.explanation: The phrase 'no more' signals that the manna ceased from that point onward — it was no longer given.

questions.question: What characteristic of the land of Canaan is suggested by this verse?
answers: A desert land without grain
A fertile land whose produce could feed the people
An isolated region without agricultural economy
questions.explanation: The verse portrays Canaan as fertile and productive — its produce could sustain the people.

paragraphs.title: The commander of the LORD's host and the holiness of the place

easy.question: What did Joshua see near Jericho according to these verses?
answers: A man standing opposite him
An approaching enemy army
A ruined city
easy.explanation: The verse says Joshua 'lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, there stood a man over against him' — a man stood before him.

easy.question: What was the man holding when he appeared before Joshua?
answers: A large staff
A sword drawn
A shield
easy.explanation: The verse describes 'and his sword drawn in his hand' — the sword was drawn.

easy.question: How did Joshua respond when the man said 'I am captain of the host of the LORD'?
answers: He began to give orders to the people
He fell on his face and worshiped
He fled from the area
easy.explanation: Joshua 'fell on his face to the earth, and did worship' — he prostrated and worshiped.

medium.question: What was Joshua asking when he said 'Art thou for us, or for our adversaries'?
answers: Whether the man was on Israel's side or their enemies
Inviting him to spend the night with Israel
Asking if he knew the way to Jerusalem
medium.explanation: Joshua was inquiring whether the figure was for Israel or for their adversaries — to learn his allegiance.

medium.question: What does 'holy' mean in the command 'for the place whereon thou standest is holy'?
answers: A special, consecrated place demanding respect
A place full of valuable objects
A place not fit to enter
medium.explanation: Here 'holy' denotes a consecrated place requiring reverence; the instruction to remove the shoe emphasizes that sanctity.

medium.question: What did Joshua do immediately after the command to loose his shoe?
answers: He obeyed and took off his shoe
He refused in protest
He continued holding his sword
medium.explanation: The verse concludes 'And Joshua did so' — he obeyed and removed his shoe.

challenge.question: Who is most likely meant by 'the captain of the host of the LORD' in the biblical tradition?
answers: The angel of the LORD or a divine messenger
A commander of Jericho's army
A neighboring king
challenge.explanation: In biblical contexts this title is usually understood as the angel of the LORD or a divine commander, not a human commander of Jericho.

challenge.question: What does removing the shoe symbolize in the cultural/religious context here?
answers: A sign of disrespect to the place
Recognition of the place's holiness and submission before the divine presence
A practical measure to improve agility in battle
challenge.explanation: Removing shoes before a holy place is a gesture of reverence and acknowledgment of the site's sacredness and the divine presence.

challenge.question: What does the detail that the man's sword was 'drawn' suggest about the encounter?
answers: That the man was a traveler in need of help
It indicates readiness for battle but also authority; yet he demands respect for the holy place
That the sword had never been used
challenge.explanation: A drawn sword shows the figure's preparedness and authoritative presence; still, he insists on recognition of the place's holiness.

answers: The angel of the LORD or a divine messenger
A commander of Jericho's army
A neighboring king
questions.explanation: In biblical contexts this title is usually understood as the angel of the LORD or a divine commander, not a human commander of Jericho.

questions.explanation: A drawn sword shows the figure's preparedness and authoritative presence; still, he insists on recognition of the place's holiness.
